q:
The committee's report was so __________ that even experts struggled to follow its argument; every paragraph seemed to loop back on itself.
Select the most appropriate option to complete the above sentence.
solution:
Clue: experts struggled to follow it and it looped back on itself ⇒ the blank means 'complicated and hard to follow'.
convoluted = extremely complex and difficult to follow ✓.
concise = brief and clear, cogent = clear and convincing — both the opposite of the clue. candid = frank, which says nothing about clarity.
Trap: 'cogent' and 'concise' look academic and suit a 'report', but their tone is positive.

q:
Unlike his __________ predecessor, who announced even minor decisions at press conferences, the new director prefers to work quietly.
Select the most appropriate option to complete the above sentence.
solution:
Contrast clue Unlike: the predecessor must be the opposite of 'prefers to work quietly' — showy and publicity-seeking.
flamboyant = showy, attention-seeking ✓.
reticent = reserved, quiet — this describes the new director, not the predecessor. diligent (hard-working) and frugal (thrifty) give no contrast with working quietly.
Trap: picking the word that fits the second half of the sentence instead of the person the blank describes.

q:
The new medicine only __________ the pain; it does nothing to cure the underlying infection.
Select the most appropriate option to complete the above sentence.
solution:
'only … ; it does nothing to cure' ⇒ the medicine gives some relief but no cure.
alleviates = makes (pain, suffering) less severe ✓.
aggravates = makes worse — then 'only' and the contrast with 'cure' make no sense. diagnoses = identifies a disease (doctors diagnose, medicines do not). transmits = passes on (a disease) — illogical for a medicine.

q:
Her __________ should not be mistaken for timidity; she simply prefers to listen carefully before she speaks.
Select the most appropriate option to complete the above sentence.
solution:
The sentence says the quality only looks like timidity but is really a preference to listen before speaking.
reserve = a tendency to keep one's thoughts and feelings to oneself, quietness ✓.
cowardice is timidity itself — the sentence says the two must not be confused. arrogance (pride) and eloquence (fluent, persuasive speech) would never be mistaken for timidity.
Trap: choosing the synonym of the word the sentence rejects.

q:
The witness's account of the accident was __________, leaving out nothing, not even the colour of the driver's shirt.
Select the most appropriate option to complete the above sentence.
solution:
Restatement clue: leaving out nothing ⇒ complete in every detail.
exhaustive = covering every detail, thorough ✓.
cursory = hasty and superficial — the opposite. inconsistent (self-contradictory) and implausible (hard to believe) describe credibility, not completeness, and nothing in the sentence supports them.

q:
The scientist was __________ about the early results: encouraged, but unwilling to claim success until the trial had been repeated.
Select the most appropriate option to complete the above sentence.
solution:
The colon explains the blank: encouraged, but unwilling to claim success = hopeful yet cautious.
guarded = cautious, not revealing or committing fully ✓.
euphoric = intensely happy — too strong; she is not claiming success. dismissive = treating as unworthy — contradicts 'encouraged'. indifferent = not caring — contradicts 'encouraged'.
Trap: matching only the first half ('encouraged') and choosing an over-strong positive word.

q:
Though he lived __________, spending almost nothing on himself, he donated generously every year to the village school.
Select the most appropriate option to complete the above sentence.
solution:
The clause spending almost nothing on himself fixes the meaning: very careful with money for himself. 'Though … he donated generously' must still be possible.
frugally = economically, avoiding waste — a neutral/positive word that says nothing against generosity ✓.
stingily = unwilling to spend or give — it contradicts the generous donations (stinginess includes meanness to others). lavishly, extravagantly = spending a lot — contradict 'spending almost nothing'.
Trap: frugal (thrifty) vs stingy/miserly (mean): the shade decides the answer.

q:
After weeks of hearings, the tribunal found the evidence __________: it neither proved nor disproved the charge.
Select the most appropriate option to complete the above sentence.
solution:
The colon restates the blank: neither proved nor disproved.
inconclusive = not leading to a firm conclusion ✓.
incriminating = suggesting guilt, irrefutable = impossible to deny — both would prove the charge. fabricated = invented; the tribunal said nothing about the evidence being false.

q:
The minister's statement was deliberately __________, worded so that both supporters and critics could read their own views into it.
Select the most appropriate option to complete the above sentence.
solution:
Clue: both sides could read their own views into it ⇒ open to more than one interpretation.
ambiguous = having more than one possible meaning ✓.
unequivocal = having only one clear meaning — the opposite. verbose = using too many words (length, not double meaning). candid = frank and honest — a frank statement would not please both sides.

q:
The once-thriving port is now __________; its warehouses stand empty and its cranes have rusted.
Select the most appropriate option to complete the above sentence.
solution:
Clue after the semicolon: empty warehouses, rusted cranes ⇒ abandoned and decaying.
derelict = in a very poor condition because of disuse and neglect ✓.
bustling = full of activity, renovated = restored, pristine = in original, unspoilt condition — all contradict the clue. 'once-thriving … now' also signals a change for the worse.

q:
The manager did not reject the plan outright, but her __________ response made it clear that she had little enthusiasm for it.
Select the most appropriate option to complete the above sentence.
solution:
Two limits: she did not reject it, yet showed little enthusiasm ⇒ a half-hearted, mildly negative response.
lukewarm = (of a response) unenthusiastic, half-hearted ✓.
effusive = gushing with enthusiasm — opposite. vehement = forceful, passionate — too strong; a vehement response would be a rejection or a strong endorsement. prompt = quick — speed, not attitude.
Trap: degree — the blank sits between support and rejection.

q:
Years of drought had __________ the soil, leaving it unable to support even the hardiest crops.
Select the most appropriate option to complete the above sentence.
solution:
Cause–effect: drought → soil unable to support even hardy crops ⇒ the soil's resources were used up.
depleted = reduced greatly in quantity or quality, exhausted ✓.
enriched (made more fertile) and irrigated (supplied with water) are the opposite of a drought's effect. cultivated = prepared and used for crops — drought does not cultivate soil.

q:
The professor's __________ comments, brief as they were, went straight to the heart of the problem.
Select the most appropriate option to complete the above sentence.
solution:
Two clues: brief and straight to the heart of the problem ⇒ sharp, clear and penetrating.
incisive = intelligently analytical and clear-thinking, cutting to the core ✓.
rambling = long and wandering — contradicts 'brief'. superficial = not going below the surface — contradicts 'heart of the problem'. insipid = dull, lacking flavour or interest.
Trap: 'brief as they were' is concessive — the comments were short yet deep, so a 'short' word alone is not enough.

q:
Instead of helping to __________ the tension between the two groups, the mediator's careless remarks only inflamed it.
Select the most appropriate option to complete the above sentence.
solution:
Contrast: Instead of …, only inflamed it ⇒ the blank is the opposite of 'inflame' — to calm or reduce tension.
defuse = reduce the danger or tension in a situation (literally, remove the fuse) ✓.
diffuse = spread over a wide area — a sound-alike; 'diffusing tension' would mean spreading it. escalate = increase — same direction as 'inflamed', so 'instead of' makes no sense. prolong = make longer — not the opposite of inflame.
Trap: the confusable pair defuse / diffuse.

q:
The novel's ending is __________; readers are still arguing about whether the hero survived the shipwreck.
Select the most appropriate option to complete the above sentence.
solution:
Clue: readers still arguing about what happened ⇒ the ending is mysterious and unclear.
enigmatic = mysterious, difficult to interpret ✓.
predictable and hackneyed (overused, unoriginal) endings leave nothing to debate. conclusive = settling the matter — the opposite of what the readers experience.

q:
His apology seemed __________; he smiled throughout and then repeated the very remark he was apologising for.
Select the most appropriate option to complete the above sentence.
solution:
Clue: smiling throughout and repeating the offending remark ⇒ he did not mean the apology.
insincere = not genuinely felt ✓.
heartfelt = deeply sincere and contrite = feeling genuine remorse — both opposite. profuse = plentiful, overflowing (a 'profuse apology' is a long, repeated one) — the sentence is about sincerity, not quantity.

q:
The tax increase was __________ rather than abrupt: it was introduced in small steps over five years.
Select the most appropriate option to complete the above sentence.
solution:
Two clues: rather than abrupt and in small steps.
incremental = increasing by small regular steps ✓.
sweeping = wide-ranging and drastic — closer to 'abrupt'. retrospective = applying to a past period. arbitrary = based on whim rather than reason. Neither describes stepwise introduction.

q:
Though the evidence against the accused was __________, the jury took three weeks to agree on a verdict.
Select the most appropriate option to complete the above sentence.
solution:
Concession clue Though: the blank must make a long deliberation surprising. That happens only if the evidence was very strong.
overwhelming = very great in amount or strength ✓.
With flimsy (weak) or circumstantial (indirect, not proving the fact directly) evidence, a long deliberation is expected, so 'Though' would be illogical. inadmissible evidence cannot be considered by the jury at all.
Trap: ignoring the contrast signal and choosing a word that merely 'goes with' long deliberation.

q:
Two candidates with identical scores received different grades because the rules were applied __________.
Select the most appropriate option to complete the above sentence.
solution:
Effect: identical scores → different grades ⇒ the rules were applied without consistent reason.
arbitrarily = based on random choice or whim, not on a fixed rule ✓.
uniformly and rigidly (strictly, without exception) would give identical scores identical grades. transparently = openly — says nothing about inconsistency.

q:
A scientist must remain __________; she cannot let her hopes about the outcome colour the way she reads the data.
Select the most appropriate option to complete the above sentence.
solution:
The clause after the semicolon defines the blank: not letting personal feelings affect judgment ⇒ objective.
dispassionate = not influenced by strong emotion; impartial ✓.
uninterested and apathetic = not interested / not caring — a scientist is expected to care about her work; she must only keep feelings out of judgment. partisan = biased in favour of one side — the opposite.
Trap: confusing 'impartial' with 'not interested'.

q:
The CEO's __________ remarks about the employees' work ethic drew sharp criticism, and she later admitted that they had been unfair.
Select all options that can fill the blank appropriately.
solution:
Clues: the remarks drew sharp criticism and were unfair ⇒ they belittled the employees.
disparaging = expressing a low opinion, belittling ✓. derogatory = showing a critical or disrespectful attitude ✓.
laudatory = expressing praise — praise would not be called unfair to the employees. conciliatory = intended to make peace — would not draw sharp criticism.

q:
The speaker's __________ manner — he never raised his voice and answered every hostile question calmly — won over the audience.
Select all options that can fill the blank appropriately.
solution:
The dashes restate the blank: never raised his voice, answered hostile questions calmly ⇒ calm under pressure.
unflappable = having or showing calm in a crisis ✓. composed = calm and in control of oneself ✓.
belligerent = hostile and aggressive, flustered = agitated and confused — both contradict the description.

q:
The critic, usually __________ in her reviews, was surprisingly __________ about the debut film, calling it the finest of the decade.
Select the most appropriate pair of words to complete the above sentence.
solution:
Polarity grid: surprisingly means the second blank contrasts with her usual style; finest of the decade makes the second blank strongly positive ⇒ blank 1 negative, blank 2 positive.
scathing = severely critical; effusive = expressing praise without restraint ✓ (−, +).
generous … lavish (+, +): no surprise. harsh … dismissive (−, −): contradicts 'finest of the decade'. lenient … critical (+, −): the second word contradicts the praise.
Shortcut: fix blank 2 from the quoted praise first; then 'surprisingly' forces blank 1 negative.

q:
Because the bridge's design had been __________ tested, the engineers were __________ when it developed cracks within a year.
Select the most appropriate pair of words to complete the above sentence.
solution:
Logic: the engineers' reaction must follow from how the design was tested. Cracks are a shock only if testing had been thorough.
rigorously = extremely thoroughly; baffled = totally puzzled ✓ — thorough testing → cracks are puzzling.
carelessly … astonished and scarcely … bewildered: after poor testing, cracks are not surprising, so the reaction does not follow. rigorously … unsurprised: thorough testing makes early cracks unexpected, so 'unsurprised' does not follow.
Trap: checking each word alone instead of the cause → effect link between the blanks.

q:
The policy was meant to __________ unemployment, but critics argue that it has only __________ the problem.
Select the most appropriate pair of words to complete the above sentence.
solution:
meant to … but … only ⇒ the intention was good and the result was bad: blank 1 = reduce, blank 2 = make worse.
alleviate = lessen; exacerbated = made worse ✓.
aggravate … mitigated and worsen … eased reverse the two meanings (no policy is meant to worsen unemployment). reduce … resolved: both positive, so 'but critics argue … only' has nothing to contrast.

q:
The auditor found the company's accounts __________: every single figure was supported by a receipt.
Select the most appropriate option to complete the above sentence.
solution:
The colon explains the blank: every figure backed by a receipt ⇒ faultless records.
impeccable = in accordance with the highest standards, flawless ✓.
fraudulent (dishonest), haphazard (lacking order) and opaque (hard to understand, not transparent) all contradict fully documented accounts.

q:
By postponing the vote yet again, the committee made a tacit admission that it did not have enough support.
Select the most appropriate option that can replace the word "tacit" without changing the meaning of the sentence.
solution:
tacit = understood or implied without being stated. Postponing the vote 'admits' the lack of support through action, not words ⇒ implied ✓.
explicit = stated clearly — the opposite of tacit. public: the committee announced nothing. reluctant = unwilling — it may well be true, but it changes the meaning (manner of admitting, not the fact that it was unspoken).
Trap: choosing a word that fits the sentence but is not a synonym of the given word.

q:
Her remarks, though brief, were pertinent to the discussion.
Select the most appropriate option that can replace the word "pertinent" without changing the meaning of the sentence.
solution:
pertinent = relevant or applicable to a particular matter ⇒ relevant ✓.
impertinent = rude, disrespectful — a look-alike with an unrelated meaning. pleasant and opposed change the meaning.
Trap: the sound-alike 'impertinent'.

q:
The old regulation became obsolete once the new act was passed.
Select the most appropriate option that can replace the word "obsolete" without changing the meaning of the sentence.
solution:
obsolete = no longer in use, out of date ⇒ outdated ✓.
obscure = not well known / unclear (a look-alike). illegal = against the law — a replaced regulation is not 'against the law', it is simply no longer used. absolute = complete, total (sound-alike).

q:
The company's profits were buoyed by an unexpected surge in exports.
Select the most appropriate option that can replace the word "buoyed" without changing the meaning of the sentence.
solution:
buoy (up) = to keep afloat; figuratively, to keep at a high level or to support and raise ⇒ profits were lifted by the export surge ✓.
weighed down = the opposite. concealed and measured do not follow from a 'surge in exports'.
Trap: the literal sense (a buoy floats) hides the figurative one; the 'surge' clue tells you the effect was upward.

q:
The manager tried to placate the angry customers by offering each of them a full refund.
Select all options that can replace the word "placate" without changing the meaning of the sentence.
solution:
placate = make (someone) less angry or hostile ⇒ pacify ✓ and appease ✓ (both = calm someone by satisfying them).
compensate = make up for a loss — the refund is compensation, but 'placate' names the aim (calming them), so the meaning changes. provoke = make angry — the opposite.
Trap: picking the word that describes the means (refund) instead of the purpose (calming).

q:
Her version of the incident was corroborated by two independent witnesses.
Select the most appropriate option that can replace the word "corroborated" without changing the meaning of the sentence.
solution:
corroborate = confirm or give support to (a statement or theory) ⇒ confirmed ✓.
contradicted = the opposite. invented = made up. reported = merely stated — witnesses who 'reported' the version need not support it.

q:
The scheme looked lucrative on paper but collapsed within a year.
Select the most appropriate option that can replace the word "lucrative" without changing the meaning of the sentence.
solution:
lucrative = producing a great deal of profit ⇒ profitable ✓.
ambitious (requiring great effort) and risky change the meaning; 'looked risky … but collapsed' would also lose the contrast signalled by but. legal is unrelated.

q:
The two sides reached a provisional agreement, subject to approval by both boards.
Select the most appropriate option that can replace the word "provisional" without changing the meaning of the sentence.
solution:
provisional = arranged for the present, possibly to be changed later ⇒ tentative ✓. The clue 'subject to approval' confirms the agreement is not yet final.
final = the opposite. professional (sound-alike start) and generous are unrelated.

q:
The minister's speech was full of platitudes and offered no concrete plans.
Select the most appropriate option that can replace the word "platitudes" without changing the meaning of the sentence.
solution:
platitude = a remark that has been used too often to be interesting or meaningful ⇒ clichés ✓. The clue 'offered no concrete plans' fits empty, overused statements.
statistics would be concrete content. insults changes the tone. promises fits the sentence grammatically but means something different — a platitude is a stale truism, not an undertaking to do something.
Trap: choosing a word that suits a political speech instead of the meaning of the given word.

q:
Her early hypothesis, ridiculed at the time, was vindicated by later and more precise experiments.
Select the most appropriate option that can replace the word "vindicated" without changing the meaning of the sentence.
solution:
vindicate = show to be right or justified, especially after doubt ⇒ proved right ✓. 'ridiculed at the time' sets up the later reversal.
disproved = the opposite. repeated and published describe what happened to experiments, not to the hypothesis's standing.

q:
Water scarcity in the region is exacerbated by poor management of the reservoirs.
Select the most appropriate option that can replace the word "exacerbated" without changing the meaning of the sentence.
solution:
exacerbate = make (a problem) worse ⇒ worsened ✓.
caused is the tempting trap: the scarcity already exists (e.g. due to low rainfall); poor management makes it worse, it does not create it — replacing the word changes the meaning. eased = the opposite. measured is unrelated.

q:
Even seasoned travellers find the mountain pass daunting in winter.
Select the most appropriate option that can replace the word "seasoned" without changing the meaning of the sentence.
solution:
Second sense: seasoned (of a person) = accustomed to particular conditions; experienced ⇒ experienced ✓. 'Even' signals that these are people who would normally cope.
spiced is the cooking sense — wrong for travellers. elderly: 'seasons' suggests years, but the word means experience, not age. wealthy is unrelated.
Trap: taking the first (cooking) meaning instead of the one the sentence needs.

q:
When asked about the leaked report, the minister said nothing at all — and his silence was telling.
Select the most appropriate option that can replace the word "telling" without changing the meaning of the sentence.
solution:
Second sense: telling (adj.) = having a striking or revealing effect; significant ⇒ his silence revealed something (that he had no good answer) ✓.
talkative is the literal 'tell' trap — and absurd for silence. misleading reverses the idea: a telling silence gives away the truth. brief says nothing about significance.

q:
The general's cavalier attitude towards his soldiers' safety cost many lives.
Select the most appropriate option that can replace the word "cavalier" without changing the meaning of the sentence.
solution:
cavalier (adj.) = showing a lack of proper concern; offhand ⇒ careless ✓. The effect 'cost many lives' confirms a negative meaning.
brave and chivalrous come from the noun sense (a cavalier = a gallant horseman) — positive, and wrong here. cautious is the opposite.
Trap: the historical noun meaning pulls towards 'brave/chivalrous'; the adjective is negative.

q:
The government's response to the flood was prompt.
Which one of the following is most nearly opposite in meaning to the word "prompt" as used in the sentence?
solution:
prompt = done without delay. Its opposite is tardy = late, slow to act ✓.
swift is a synonym (the standard trap in antonym questions). accurate and rude are on different scales.

q:
Her views on economic policy are thoroughly orthodox.
Which one of the following is most nearly opposite in meaning to the word "orthodox" as used in the sentence?
solution:
orthodox = following generally accepted beliefs; conventional. Opposite: unconventional ✓.
traditional is a synonym. religious comes from the narrower religious sense of 'orthodox', which does not apply to economic policy. popular is on a different scale (orthodox views may or may not be popular).

q:
The scarcity of skilled workers delayed the project by a year.
Which one of the following is most nearly opposite in meaning to the word "scarcity" as used in the sentence?
solution:
scarcity = insufficiency, shortness of supply. Opposite: abundance = a very large quantity ✓.
paucity and shortage are synonyms. quality concerns how good the workers are, not how many there are.

q:
Fame earned on social media is often ephemeral.
Which one of the following is most nearly opposite in meaning to the word "ephemeral" as used in the sentence?
solution:
ephemeral = lasting for a very short time. Opposite: enduring = lasting a long time ✓.
fleeting is a synonym. ethereal = extremely delicate, heavenly — a sound-alike with an unrelated meaning. famous repeats the subject of the sentence, not the opposite of the word.

q:
The victor was magnanimous towards his defeated rival.
Which one of the following is most nearly opposite in meaning to the word "magnanimous" as used in the sentence?
solution:
magnanimous = generous or forgiving, especially towards a rival or less powerful person. Opposite: petty = mean-spirited, small-minded ✓.
generous is a synonym. magnificent is a look-alike (both from Latin magnus, great) but means impressive. humble = modest — not the opposite of being forgiving.

q:
Match the words in the first column with their synonyms in the second column.
(i) Candid   (ii) Lethargic   (iii) Meticulous   (iv) Ominous
(p) Sluggish   (q) Threatening   (r) Frank   (s) Thorough
solution:
Candid = frank, open (r). Lethargic = sluggish, lacking energy (p). Meticulous = very careful and precise, thorough (s). Ominous = giving the impression that something bad will happen; threatening (q).
So (i)-(r); (ii)-(p); (iii)-(s); (iv)-(q).
Shortcut: lock the sure pairs Candid–Frank and Ominous–Threatening; then Lethargic–Sluggish leaves Meticulous–Thorough.

q:
Match the words in the first column with their antonyms in the second column.
(i) Frugal   (ii) Benevolent   (iii) Lucid   (iv) Ascend
(p) Malicious   (q) Descend   (r) Obscure   (s) Extravagant
solution:
Frugal (thrifty) ↔ Extravagant (spending too much) (s). Benevolent (kind, well-meaning) ↔ Malicious (intending harm) (p). Lucid (clear, easy to understand) ↔ Obscure (unclear) (r). Ascend ↔ Descend (q).
So (i)-(s); (ii)-(p); (iii)-(r); (iv)-(q).
Shortcut: Ascend–Descend is in every option, so decide Frugal first: only the extravagant pairing is an opposite.

q: Which one of the following words is not a synonym of "diligent" as used in the sentence: "The diligent clerk checked every entry twice."
solution:
diligent = showing care and effort in one's work. industrious, painstaking and hardworking are all synonyms.
indolent = lazy, avoiding effort — an antonym, so it is the word that is not a synonym ✓.
Trap: 'indolent' and 'industrious' both start with 'ind-'; read the meaning, not the shape.

q:
"The obstinate child refused to eat anything except plain rice."
Select all words that are synonyms of "obstinate" as used in the sentence.
solution:
obstinate = stubbornly refusing to change one's opinion or course of action.
stubborn ✓ and headstrong (self-willed, determined to do as one wants) ✓ are synonyms.
docile = ready to accept control, obedient, and pliant = easily influenced, flexible — both antonyms.

q:
"The selection process for the scholarship was entirely transparent."
Select all words that are opposite in meaning to "transparent" as used in the sentence.
solution:
Here transparent (of a process) = open to public scrutiny, nothing hidden.
opaque = (of a process) not open, hard to understand or see into ✓; secretive = inclined to conceal ✓. Both are opposites.
open and candid (frank) are synonyms.
Trap: 'opaque' is usually learnt in its physical sense (not letting light through) but carries the same figurative sense as transparent.

q:
The professor's lecture was so soporific that half the class dozed off.
Which one of the following is closest in meaning to "soporific" as used in the sentence?
solution:
soporific = tending to induce drowsiness or sleep ⇒ sleep-inducing ✓ (the effect 'dozed off' confirms it).
stimulating is the opposite. A confusing or lengthy lecture might make students sleepy, but these describe different qualities and are not the meaning of the word.

q:
Even after the surgery, the old man's walk remained slow and laboured.
Which one of the following is most nearly opposite in meaning to the word "laboured" as used in the sentence?
solution:
laboured = done with great difficulty, showing effort. Opposite: effortless = requiring no physical or mental exertion ✓.
strenuous (requiring great effort) is a synonym. sluggish (slow-moving) echoes 'slow' in the sentence — also not an opposite. elderly describes the man, not his walk.

q:
The firm's fortunes began to wane after its founder retired.
Which one of the following is closest in meaning to "wane" as used in the sentence?
solution:
wane = decrease in vigour, power or extent ⇒ decline ✓ (the moon wanes when it shrinks).
wax = grow (the moon waxes) — the opposite. recover is also opposite in direction. fluctuate = rise and fall irregularly — not a steady decline.

q:
Throughout the tense meeting, the union leader's tone remained conciliatory.
Which one of the following is most nearly opposite in meaning to the word "conciliatory" as used in the sentence?
solution:
conciliatory = intended to placate or pacify; seeking to end disagreement. Opposite: confrontational = tending to deal with situations aggressively ✓.
placatory is a synonym. apologetic is close in spirit (seeking peace), not opposite. indifferent = not caring — it is neither peace-seeking nor hostile, so it is not the opposite.

q:
"The new rules will not __________ students who have already registered; their main __________ will be on next year's batch."
The words that best fill the blanks in the above sentence are
solution:
Blank 1 follows 'will not' ⇒ a verb: affect = to influence. Blank 2 follows 'their main' ⇒ a noun: effect = a result or influence.
So: affect, effect.
Rule: affect is normally the verb, effect the noun ('the effect of the rule'). Swapping them or repeating one word breaks the part of speech in one blank.

q:
"The __________ reason for rejecting the proposal was that it violated the basic __________ of fairness."
The words that best fill the blanks in the above sentence are
solution:
Blank 1 is an adjective before 'reason': principal = main, most important. Blank 2 is a noun meaning a rule or belief: principle = a fundamental truth or rule of conduct.
So: principal, principle.
Memory aid: a principle is a rule; the principal is your 'pal' at the head of the school / the main one.

q:
"The new curtains __________ the colour of the walls perfectly, and every guest paid us a __________ on our choice."
The words that best fill the blanks in the above sentence are
solution:
Blank 1: curtains that go well with the walls ⇒ complement = complete or enhance by adding a contrasting or matching quality. Blank 2: guests praising ⇒ compliment = an expression of praise ('pay a compliment').
So: complement, compliment.
Memory aid: complement completes; compliment = I like it.

q:
"The truck was __________ at the signal when it was hit from behind; it was carrying a load of office __________."
The words that best fill the blanks in the above sentence are
solution:
Blank 1 describes the truck at a signal ⇒ stationary (adj.) = not moving. Blank 2 is a load of goods ⇒ stationery (n.) = paper, pens and other writing materials.
So: stationary, stationery.
Memory aid: stationery has e as in envelope; stationary = standing still.

q:
"The sensor records readings at __________ intervals of ten minutes, and the researchers have promised to be __________ about the participants' identities."
The words that best fill the blanks in the above sentence are
solution:
Blank 1: separate, distinct intervals ⇒ discrete = individually separate and distinct. Blank 2: careful not to reveal identities ⇒ discreet = careful and tactful in what one says, to avoid causing offence or revealing secrets.
So: discrete, discreet.
Memory aid: in discrete the two e's are kept separate by the t.

q:
"The farmer, __________ to taking risks, insured his crop against __________ weather."
The words that best fill the blanks in the above sentence are
solution:
Blank 1 is followed by 'to taking risks' ⇒ averse (to) = having a strong dislike of or opposition to. Blank 2 describes weather ⇒ adverse = harmful, unfavourable.
So: averse, adverse.
Rule: people are averse to things; conditions, effects and weather are adverse.

q:
"Despite repeated questioning, the police could not __________ any information about the __________ trade in wildlife."
The words that best fill the blanks in the above sentence are
solution:
Blank 1 is a verb meaning 'draw out' (information) ⇒ elicit. Blank 2 describes a trade ⇒ illicit = forbidden by law.
So: elicit, illicit.
Memory aid: elicit = extract; illicit = illegal.

q:
"The board refused to __________ any scene of the documentary, but Parliament later passed a motion of __________ against the minister who had approved its release."
The words that best fill the blanks in the above sentence are
solution:
Blank 1: removing scenes from a film ⇒ censor = examine and suppress unacceptable parts. Blank 2: a formal expression of disapproval by Parliament ⇒ censure = strong formal criticism ('a motion of censure').
So: censor, censure.
Trap: both come from the same root and are pronounced alike; censor acts on content, censure on a person's conduct.

q:
"The doctor will __________ a mild painkiller, because the new law __________ the sale of the stronger drug without a special licence."
The words that best fill the blanks in the above sentence are
solution:
Blank 1: what a doctor does with a medicine ⇒ prescribe = recommend and authorise the use of. Blank 2: what a law does to a sale 'without a licence' ⇒ proscribes = forbids, especially by law.
So: prescribe, proscribes.
Trap: the two words differ by one letter but are near-opposites: pre- scribe (write before = direct), pro- scribe (publish as forbidden).

q:
"The report does not state it directly, but it __________ that the dam was poorly built; most readers will __________ that the contractor was negligent."
The words that best fill the blanks in the above sentence are
solution:
The writer (the report) suggests without stating ⇒ implies. The readers draw a conclusion from what they read ⇒ infer.
So: implies, infer.
Rule: the speaker/writer implies; the listener/reader infers.

q:
"The patient needs a __________ supply of oxygen through the night, without even a moment's break."
The word that best fills the blank in the above sentence is
solution:
'without even a moment's break' ⇒ continuous = forming an unbroken whole, without interruption ✓.
continual = happening repeatedly with breaks in between ('continual interruptions'). contiguous = sharing a common border, touching. consecutive = following one after another in order (used for separate items: 'three consecutive days').
Rule: continuous = one unbroken stretch; continual = always recurring.

q:
"A judge must be __________ in every case she hears: she must have nothing to gain from either verdict."
The word that best fills the blank in the above sentence is
solution:
The colon defines the blank: having nothing to gain from the outcome ⇒ disinterested = not influenced by personal advantage; impartial ✓.
uninterested = not interested, bored — a judge must pay close attention, so this is wrong. interested (in the legal sense: having a stake) is the opposite of what is required. disenchanted = disappointed, disillusioned.
Trap: disinterested (impartial) vs uninterested (bored).

q:
"Only a __________ reader would accept the advertisement's claim that the cream can reverse ten years of ageing in a week."
The word that best fills the blank in the above sentence is
solution:
Someone who would 'accept' an absurd claim is too ready to believe ⇒ credulous = having too great a readiness to believe things ✓.
credible = believable — it describes a claim, not a reader ('a credible reader' does not mean one who believes easily). creditable = deserving praise. critical reader would reject the claim — the opposite.
Trap: credible (can be believed) vs credulous (believes too easily).

q:
"The engineer's __________ design halved the building's water use by relying only on gravity."
The word that best fills the blank in the above sentence is
solution:
A clever, inventive design ⇒ ingenious = clever, original and inventive ✓.
ingenuous = innocent and unsuspecting, naive — said of people. indigenous = native to a place. ingenuity is the noun (cleverness), so it cannot describe 'design'.
Trap: ingenious (clever) vs ingenuous (naive).

q:
"With black clouds gathering over the hills, a storm seemed __________."
The word that best fills the blank in the above sentence is
solution:
Gathering clouds signal something about to happen ⇒ imminent = about to happen ✓.
eminent = famous and respected (of a person). prominent = important or noticeable. permanent = lasting for ever — storms are not.
Trap: imminent / eminent are near-homophones.

q:
"Of the two proposals, the __________ was cheaper, so the committee approved it __________ that week."
The words that best fill the blanks in the above sentence are
solution:
Blank 1: the second of two things just mentioned ⇒ latter. Blank 2: an adverb of time ⇒ later = afterwards.
So: latter, later.
Rule: former / latter pick out one of two; later refers to time.

q:
"Drivers who __________ traffic rules should be fined, and must not be allowed to __________ their political connections to escape the penalty."
The words that best fill the blanks in the above sentence are
solution:
Blank 1: openly disregarding rules ⇒ flout = openly disregard (a rule or law). Blank 2: displaying connections ostentatiously ⇒ flaunt = display something ostentatiously, show off.
So: flout, flaunt.
Trap: 'flaunting the rules' is a common error; you flout rules and flaunt wealth or connections.

q: Select all sentences in which the underlined word is used correctly.
options: The <u>principal</u> of the school addressed the students at the assembly.
She refused to compromise on her <u>principals</u>, even under pressure.
The <u>principal</u> amount of the loan was repaid in five years.
The <u>principle</u> cause of the delay was the heavy rain.
solution:
principal = (n.) the head of a school; the original sum of a loan; (adj.) main. principle = a fundamental rule or belief.
(A) head of the school ⇒ principal ✓. (C) the original sum lent ⇒ principal ✓.
(B) beliefs one refuses to compromise ⇒ should be principles ✗. (D) 'main cause' is an adjective ⇒ should be principal ✗.
Trap: 'principal' has three senses (head, main, capital sum); 'principle' has only the 'rule/belief' sense.

q: Select all sentences in which the underlined word is used correctly.
options: The medicine took <u>effect</u> within an hour.
The transport strike will <u>effect</u> thousands of daily commuters.
The new manager <u>effected</u> several changes in her very first month.
Cold weather can <u>affect</u> a battery's performance.
solution:
affect (v.) = influence; effect (n.) = result; effect (v.) = bring about, cause to happen.
(A) 'take effect' = come into operation — noun ✓. (C) 'effected several changes' = brought them about — the verb effect ✓. (D) cold influences performance ⇒ affect ✓.
(B) the strike will influence commuters ⇒ should be affect ✗.
Trap: assuming 'effect' can never be a verb — 'effect a change' is standard.

q:
After two years of trying to save the loss-making factory, the owners finally __________ and put it up for sale.
Select the most appropriate option to complete the above sentence.
options: let the cat out of the bag
solution:
throw in the towel = admit defeat, give up ✓ — after two years of trying, they stopped and sold the factory.
burn the midnight oil = work late into the night. let the cat out of the bag = reveal a secret. beat around the bush = avoid the main point. None of these means giving up.

q:
The new stadium, which costs crores every year to maintain but hosts barely two matches, has become a white elephant.
The idiom "white elephant" in the above sentence means
options: a costly possession that is of little use
solution:
a white elephant = a possession whose cost (of upkeep) is out of proportion to its usefulness ✓. The sentence itself explains: huge maintenance cost, barely used.
'rare and valuable asset' and 'symbol of national pride' are positive and contradict the context. 'painted white' is the literal trap.

q:
When the reporters asked about the delays, the spokesperson kept beating around the bush.
The idiom "beating around the bush" in the above sentence means
solution:
beat around (about) the bush = discuss a matter without coming to the point ✓.
The idiom says nothing about anger, blaming anyone or searching — those add meanings that are not in the phrase.

q:
Ravi got cold feet on the morning of his presentation and asked a colleague to deliver it instead.
The idiom "got cold feet" in the above sentence means
solution:
get cold feet = lose one's nerve or confidence just before doing something planned ✓ — which is why he handed the presentation over.
'fell ill with a chill' is the literal trap. 'prepared thoroughly' contradicts backing out. 'arrived late' is not implied.

q:
The detective soon realised that the torn letter found near the body was a red herring.
The idiom "red herring" in the above sentence means
options: a clue meant to divert attention from the truth
the most important piece of evidence
solution:
a red herring = something, especially a clue, that is misleading or distracting ✓. 'soon realised' suggests the letter first seemed important and then proved misleading.
'the most important evidence' is the opposite. 'sign of danger' confuses it with a red flag. 'coded message' is unrelated.
Trap: red herring (false lead) vs red flag (warning sign).

q:
Meera visits her hometown only __________; the last time she went was three years ago.
Select the most appropriate option to complete the above sentence.
solution:
The clue 'the last time … three years ago' ⇒ very rarely. once in a blue moon = very rarely ✓.
every now and then = occasionally, fairly often — too frequent. day in and day out = every day, continuously. round the clock = all day and night.

q:
The proposal looked attractive, but the finance team advised us to take its revenue projections __________, since the same firm had overestimated its numbers before.
Select the most appropriate option to complete the above sentence.
solution:
Clue: the firm had overestimated before ⇒ do not fully believe the projections. take something with a pinch of salt = regard it as exaggerated; believe only part of it ✓.
take at face value = accept as true without question — the opposite. take by storm = capture or win over quickly. take in one's stride = deal with calmly.
Trap: all four begin with 'take'; only one carries doubt.

q:
Losing that job turned out to be __________: it pushed Arjun to start the business that later made him successful.
Select the most appropriate option to complete the above sentence.
solution:
The colon explains the blank: a loss that led to success ⇒ a blessing in disguise = something that seems bad at first but turns out to be good ✓.
a bolt from the blue = a sudden, unexpected event — it describes surprise, not the good outcome the colon explains. a storm in a teacup = great anger about a trivial matter. a cock-and-bull story = an absurd, unbelievable explanation.

q:
The inspection committee accused the contractor of __________ by using cheaper cement than the contract specified.
Select the most appropriate option to complete the above sentence.
solution:
Using cheaper material than specified = doing a job badly to save money. cut corners = do something perfunctorily or badly to save time or money ✓.
break the ice = ease tension when people first meet. toe the line = obey the rules — the opposite. turn the tables = reverse one's position relative to someone.

q:
The company pays only __________ to safety: the rules exist on paper, but nobody ever enforces them.
Select the most appropriate option to complete the above sentence.
solution:
The colon gives the clue: rules exist only on paper ⇒ support in words, not in action. pay lip service to = express approval or support without acting on it ✓.
pay heed to = pay careful attention — that would mean the rules are followed. pay tribute / homage to = honour or praise publicly — the sentence is about hollow support, not praise.
Trap: all four collocate with 'pay'; only 'lip service' carries the sense of empty words.

q:
Both teams had lost their best players to injury, so neither could complain: they were __________.
Select the most appropriate option to complete the above sentence.
solution:
Both teams face the same difficulty ⇒ in the same boat = in the same difficult circumstances as others ✓.
on the fence = undecided. at loggerheads = in strong disagreement (the injuries do not cause a quarrel). over the moon = extremely happy — contradicts losing the best players.

q:
The board is still __________ about the merger: it has not yet decided whether to support or oppose it.
Select the most appropriate option to complete the above sentence.
solution:
The colon defines the blank: not yet decided ⇒ on the fence = undecided, not committed to either side ✓.
up in arms = protesting angrily — a definite position. in the dark = uninformed — the board knows about the merger; it simply has not decided. over the moon = delighted.

q:
When the consultant said that the real problem was poor communication between departments, she hit the nail on the head.
The idiom "hit the nail on the head" in the above sentence means
solution:
hit the nail on the head = describe exactly what is causing a situation or problem ✓.
'criticised harshly' takes 'hit' literally. 'avoided the main issue' is the opposite (that is beating around the bush). 'made it worse' is unrelated.

q: Select all sentences in which the idiom is used appropriately.
options: Anita burnt the midnight oil all week before the exam and passed comfortably.
Rohan let the cat out of the bag by telling his sister about her surprise birthday party.
The old car is his Achilles' heel; he proudly drives it everywhere because it never breaks down.
Having turned a blind eye to the leaking pipe, the manager had it repaired immediately.
solution:
(A) burn the midnight oil = work late into the night ✓ — fits studying before an exam.
(B) let the cat out of the bag = reveal a secret by mistake ✓ — he revealed the surprise.
(C) Achilles' heel = a weakness or vulnerable point; a reliable car he is proud of is not a weakness ✗.
(D) turn a blind eye = deliberately ignore; ignoring the leak contradicts repairing it immediately ✗.
Trap: each wrong sentence uses the idiom with a context that reverses its meaning.

q:
Because of heavy rain, the final match was __________ and it will not be played at all this season.
Select the most appropriate option to complete the above sentence.
solution:
'will not be played at all' ⇒ cancelled. call off = cancel ✓.
put off = postpone — a postponed match would be played later, contradicting the sentence. call on = visit or ask someone to do something. put out = extinguish (a fire) or inconvenience.
Trap: call off (cancel) vs put off (postpone).

q:
The meeting has been __________ to next Monday because the chairperson is travelling this week.
Select the most appropriate option to complete the above sentence.
solution:
'to next Monday' ⇒ moved to a later date. put off = postpone ✓.
called off = cancelled — a cancelled meeting is not moved 'to next Monday'. put up = build, display, or accommodate. set off = begin a journey or trigger.

q:
I can no longer __________ the noise from the construction site next door; I am moving out.
Select the most appropriate option to complete the above sentence.
solution:
put up with = tolerate ✓ — 'can no longer tolerate … I am moving out'.
put down to = attribute to. make up for = compensate for. come up with = think of (an idea). None fits enduring a nuisance.

q:
The committee will __________ the complaint and report its findings within a month.
Select the most appropriate option to complete the above sentence.
solution:
Examining a complaint and reporting findings ⇒ look into = investigate ✓.
look after = take care of. look up to = admire and respect. look out = be careful (and it takes no object here).

q:
Despite strong pressure from the union, the management refused to __________ on its decision to extend working hours.
Select the most appropriate option to complete the above sentence.
solution:
Refusing to yield under pressure ⇒ back down (on) = withdraw a claim or position; concede ✓.
back up = support, or make a copy. give out = stop working / distribute. take off = leave the ground / become successful. None means yielding.

q:
She __________ her grandmother: she has the same sharp wit and the same love of music.
Select the most appropriate option to complete the above sentence.
solution:
Sharing traits with an older relative ⇒ take after = resemble (a parent or ancestor) ✓.
look after = take care of. take over = assume control of. look up = search for (information) or improve.

q:
We __________ petrol on the highway and had to walk to the nearest village.
Select the most appropriate option to complete the above sentence.
solution:
Having to walk ⇒ the supply was used up. run out of = use up the supply of ✓.
run into = meet by chance or collide with. run over = knock down with a vehicle. run across = find by chance.

q:
The government plans to __________ the old paper-based licensing system and replace it with an online one.
Select the most appropriate option to complete the above sentence.
solution:
Replacing an old system ⇒ abolishing it. do away with = abolish, get rid of ✓.
do up = fasten or renovate. make up for = compensate for. put through = connect (a call) or make someone undergo something.

q:
The deal __________ at the last minute when the buyer failed to arrange the funds.
Select the most appropriate option to complete the above sentence.
solution:
A deal that does not happen because funds were not arranged ⇒ fall through = fail to happen or be completed ✓.
fall out = quarrel (people fall out, deals do not). fall back = retreat. fall for = be deceived by, or fall in love with.

q:
The new forensic report does not __________ the witness's earlier statement; in fact, it flatly contradicts it.
Select the most appropriate option to complete the above sentence.
solution:
'does not … ; in fact, it contradicts it' ⇒ the blank means 'confirm'. bear out = support or confirm (a statement or theory) ✓.
bear with = be patient with. bear down (on) = press or move towards threateningly. bear up = remain cheerful under hardship. None means 'confirm'.

q:
Her excuse that the train had been late did not __________ to scrutiny, because every train on that line had run on time that day.
Select the most appropriate option to complete the above sentence.
solution:
An excuse that fails when checked ⇒ stand up (to scrutiny) = remain valid when examined ✓.
stand by = support or be ready. stand out = be noticeable. stand down = resign from a position. Only 'stand up to scrutiny' is the fixed expression meaning 'survive examination'.

q: Select all sentences in which the phrasal verb is used with its correct meaning.
options: She turned down the job offer because the salary was too low.
The doctor told him to cut down on sugar, so he started eating more sweets.
The fire brigade put out the fire within an hour.
He looked down upon his teachers and always followed their advice respectfully.
solution:
(A) turn down = reject ✓ — rejecting a poorly paid offer.
(C) put out = extinguish ✓.
(B) cut down on = reduce; eating more sweets contradicts it ✗.
(D) look down upon = regard as inferior, despise; that contradicts following their advice respectfully ✗.

q: Which one of the following words best describes a person who can speak several languages fluently?
solution:
polyglot (poly = many, glot = tongue) = a person who knows and is able to use several languages ✓.
polymath = a person with knowledge of many subjects. bibliophile = a lover of books. orator = a skilful public speaker — skill in speaking, not in many languages.
Trap: polyglot vs polymath — both begin with 'poly-'.

q: Which one of the following words best describes a remedy for all diseases or difficulties?
solution:
panacea (pan = all) = a solution or remedy for all difficulties or diseases ✓.
placebo = a harmless substance with no medical effect, given for psychological benefit. antidote = a medicine that counteracts a particular poison. vaccine = a preparation that protects against a particular disease.
Trap: antidote and vaccine are specific; the definition says 'all'.

q:
Smartphones have become __________ in Indian cities; one sees them in every shop, bus and classroom.
Select the word that means present or found everywhere and completes the sentence.
solution:
ubiquitous = present, appearing or found everywhere ✓ — 'in every shop, bus and classroom'.
unanimous = fully in agreement. ambiguous = open to more than one interpretation. superfluous = unnecessary, more than enough. All end in '-ous' but none means 'everywhere'.

q: Which one of the following words best describes handwriting that cannot be read?
solution:
illegible (il- not + legible readable) = not clear enough to be read ✓.
ineligible = not qualified or allowed (a look-alike). illiterate = unable to read — it describes a person, not handwriting. inaudible = cannot be heard.
Trap: illegible / ineligible differ by only a few letters.

q: Which one of the following words best describes a government or society controlled by the wealthy?
solution:
plutocracy (Greek ploutos = wealth) = government by the wealthy ✓.
oligarchy = rule by a small group — the group need not be rich, so it does not capture 'the wealthy'. autocracy = rule by one person with absolute power. theocracy = rule by religious leaders.
Trap: oligarchy (few) is close but the defining feature here is wealth.

q: Which one of the following words best describes the practice among those in power of giving jobs and favours to their relatives?
solution:
nepotism (Latin nepos = nephew) = favouring relatives, especially by giving them jobs ✓.
chauvinism = excessive or prejudiced loyalty to one's own group or gender. bureaucracy = administration by officials, often with excessive procedure. philanthropy = generous help to others, especially by donating money.

q: Which one of the following words best describes a speech delivered without any preparation?
solution:
extempore = spoken or done without preparation ✓.
soliloquy = a speech in a play in which a character speaks his thoughts aloud while alone. monologue = a long speech by one person — it may be fully prepared. eulogy = a speech praising someone, typically one who has died.
Trap: monologue describes the number of speakers, not lack of preparation.

q: Which one of the following words best describes something that belongs to a period other than the one in which it is shown, such as a wristwatch on a soldier in a film set in ancient Rome?
solution:
anachronism (ana = against, chronos = time) = a thing belonging or appropriate to a period other than that in which it exists ✓.
anomaly = anything that deviates from what is normal — far too general; the definition specifically concerns being out of its time. chronicle = a record of events in time order (shares the root 'chron'). paradox = a seemingly self-contradictory statement.
Trap: 'anomaly' is true of the wristwatch, but it does not name the time error that the definition describes.

q: Which one of the following words best describes a person who is new to and inexperienced in an activity?
solution:
novice = a person new to or inexperienced in a field ✓.
amateur = a person who does something for pleasure rather than as a paid job — an amateur may be very experienced, so 'new' is not its meaning. veteran = a person with long experience (opposite). connoisseur = an expert judge of matters of taste.
Trap: amateur (not paid) vs novice (not experienced).

q: Which one of the following words best describes a mild or indirect word used in place of one considered harsh, such as 'passed away' for 'died'?
solution:
euphemism (eu = good, pheme = speaking) = a mild or indirect expression substituted for a harsh or blunt one ✓.
hyperbole = deliberate exaggeration. metaphor = describing one thing as if it were another. irony = expressing meaning using language that normally signifies the opposite.

q: Which one of the following words best describes a list of items to be discussed at a meeting, prepared beforehand?
solution:
agenda = a list of items to be discussed at a formal meeting ✓.
minutes = the written record of what was said and decided, made during/after the meeting — the definition says 'beforehand'. itinerary = a planned route or travel schedule. inventory = a complete list of items such as goods in stock.
Trap: agenda (before) vs minutes (after).

q:
Despite repeated warnings and punishments, the boy kept skipping school; his exasperated teachers finally called him __________.
Select the word that means not able to be corrected or reformed and completes the sentence.
solution:
incorrigible (in- not + corrigible correctable) = not able to be corrected or reformed ✓ — repeated warnings had no effect.
infallible = incapable of making mistakes. invincible = too powerful to be defeated. indelible = cannot be removed or erased (ink, memory). All begin with 'in-' = not, so the root decides.

q:
Consider the words: (i) tepid   (ii) scalding   (iii) cold   (iv) hot
Select the option that arranges them in increasing order of temperature.
solution:
cold (low temperature) < tepid (only slightly warm, lukewarm) < hot < scalding (hot enough to burn the skin).
So (iii), (i), (iv), (ii).
The last distractor is the decreasing order — a common slip when the question says 'increasing'.

q:
Consider the words: (i) colossal   (ii) minuscule   (iii) sizeable   (iv) small
Select the option that arranges them in increasing order of size.
solution:
minuscule = extremely small < small < sizeable = fairly large < colossal = extremely large.
So (ii), (iv), (iii), (i).
Trap: treating 'minuscule' as merely 'small'; it is the extreme of smallness.

q:
Consider the words: (i) terrified   (ii) uneasy   (iii) unperturbed   (iv) frightened
Select the option that arranges them in increasing order of fear.
solution:
unperturbed = not worried at all (no fear) < uneasy = slightly anxious < frightened = afraid < terrified = extremely afraid.
So (iii), (ii), (iv), (i).
Trap: 'unperturbed' begins with a negative prefix and is easily misread as a form of fear; it is the absence of fear, so it comes first.

q:
Consider the words: (i) condemn   (ii) praise   (iii) accept   (iv) criticise
Select the option that arranges them from the most favourable to the least favourable judgment.
solution:
praise = express warm approval (most favourable) > accept = agree to, neutral approval > criticise = point out faults > condemn = express complete, strong disapproval (least favourable).
So (ii), (iii), (iv), (i).
Trap: the last option is the right list in the reverse direction (least to most).

q:
Consider the words: (i) soaked   (ii) dry   (iii) damp   (iv) wet
Select the option that arranges them in increasing order of wetness.
solution:
dry (no moisture) < damp (slightly wet) < wet < soaked (extremely wet, saturated).
So (ii), (iii), (iv), (i).

q:
Consider the words: (i) sprint   (ii) amble   (iii) jog   (iv) walk
Select the option that arranges them in increasing order of speed.
solution:
amble = walk at a slow, relaxed pace < walk (normal pace) < jog = run at a steady, gentle pace < sprint = run at full speed over a short distance.
So (ii), (iv), (iii), (i).
Trap: placing 'amble' after 'walk' — an amble is a slow walk.

q: Which one of the following words expresses the strongest degree of dislike?
solution:
Scale of dislike: reluctance (unwillingness; hardly dislike) < distaste (mild dislike) < aversion (strong dislike) < loathing (intense dislike mixed with disgust) ✓.
Trap: 'aversion' is strong, but 'loathing' is the extreme of the scale.

q:
The handwriting on the old letter had faded so badly that I could barely __________ a single word.
Select the most appropriate option to complete the above sentence.
solution:
Struggling to read faded writing ⇒ make out = manage to see, hear or read with difficulty ✓.
make up = invent, or become friends again. make off = leave hurriedly, especially to escape. make over = transfer ownership, or renovate.

q:
"The team's __________ was low after the heavy defeat, so the coach asked the players what __________ they could draw from the loss."
The words that best fill the blanks in the above sentence are
solution:
Blank 1: the confidence and spirit of a group ⇒ morale (stress on the second syllable). Blank 2: a lesson to be learnt ⇒ moral ('the moral of the story').
So: morale, moral.
Rule: morale = team spirit; moral = a lesson (noun) or concerned with right and wrong (adjective).

q:
Select the word that completes the analogy:
Loom : Weaver :: Anvil : __________
solution:
Bridge: a weaver works at a loom (tool : worker who uses it). A blacksmith hammers metal on an anvil ✓.
A potter uses a wheel and kiln, a tailor a needle or sewing machine, a mason a trowel — none uses an anvil.

q:
Select the word that completes the analogy:
Bibliophile : Books :: Philatelist : __________
solution:
Bridge: a bibliophile is a lover/collector of books. A philatelist collects and studies postage stamps ✓.
coins → numismatist; wines → oenophile; birds → ornithologist (study) or birdwatcher.
Trap: both stamps and coins are collector's items; only 'philatelist' names stamps.

q:
Select the word that completes the analogy:
Cardiologist : Heart :: Nephrologist : __________
solution:
Bridge: a cardiologist is a doctor who specialises in the heart. A nephrologist specialises in the kidneys ✓ (Greek nephros = kidney).
nerves → neurologist (sound-alike 'ne-'); skin → dermatologist; lungs → pulmonologist.

q:
Select the word that completes the analogy:
Friction : Heat :: Evaporation : __________
solution:
Bridge: friction produces heat (process : the effect it produces). Evaporation produces cooling ✓ — the evaporating liquid takes heat from its surroundings (which is why sweat cools the body).
condensation is the opposite process, not its effect. boiling causes evaporation — the direction is reversed (cause, not effect). ice forms by freezing, not by evaporation.
Trap: picking a word merely associated with evaporation instead of what evaporation produces.

q:
Select the word that completes the analogy:
Hill : Mountain :: Stream : __________
solution:
Bridge: a mountain is a much larger hill (smaller : larger of the same kind). A river is a much larger stream ✓.
valley is a landform, not flowing water. pond is still water. spring is the source of a stream, not a larger stream.

q:
Select the word that completes the analogy:
Frugal : Extravagant :: Timid : __________
solution:
Bridge: frugal (thrifty) is the opposite of extravagant (wasteful). The opposite of timid (lacking courage) is bold ✓.
shy and cautious are near-synonyms of timid. weak is a different scale (strength).

q:
Select the word that completes the analogy:
Lucid : Clear :: Cogent : __________
solution:
Bridge: lucid means clear (synonyms). cogent (of an argument) = clear, logical and convincing ✓.
confusing is closer to the opposite. cognate = related in origin (a sound-alike). concise = brief — a cogent argument need not be short.

q:
Select the word that completes the analogy:
Composer : Symphony :: Choreographer : __________
solution:
Bridge: a composer creates a symphony (creator : work created). A choreographer creates (designs) a dance ✓.
orchestra performs a symphony — it belongs with the first pair's field, not the creator's work. stage is where a dance is performed; audience watches it.

q:
Select the word that completes the analogy:
Anonymous : Name :: Amorphous : __________
solution:
Bridge: anonymous = without a name (adjective : the thing it lacks). amorphous (a- without + morph form) = without a definite shape ✓.
love is the sound trap ('amour'). colour and mass are not what 'amorphous' denies — an amorphous solid has both colour and mass.

q:
Select the word that completes the analogy:
Insipid : Flavour :: Listless : __________
solution:
Bridge: insipid food lacks flavour (adjective : the quality it lacks). A listless person lacks energy or enthusiasm ✓.
list is a spelling trap. sadness may accompany listlessness but is not what is lacking. taste belongs to the first pair's meaning.

q:
Select the word that completes the analogy:
Odometer : Distance :: Hygrometer : __________
solution:
Bridge: an odometer measures the distance travelled (instrument : quantity measured). A hygrometer measures humidity (moisture in the air) ✓ (Greek hygros = wet).
height → altimeter; rainfall → rain gauge; temperature → thermometer.

q: Select the pair that best expresses a relationship similar to that expressed in the pair Flock : Sheep.
solution:
Bridge: a flock is a group of sheep (collective noun : members). A pride is a group of lions ✓.
Bee : Hive = animal : home. Lion : Cub = adult : young. Herd : Shepherd = group : the person who tends it (and a shepherd tends a flock).

q:
Select the word that completes the analogy:
Quiver : Arrows :: Scabbard : __________
solution:
Bridge: a quiver is a case that holds arrows (container : thing held). A scabbard is a sheath that holds a sword ✓.
bow shoots arrows but is not kept in a scabbard; shield and helmet are armour, not held in a sheath.

q:
Select the word that completes the analogy:
Ornithology : Birds :: Seismology : __________
solution:
Bridge: ornithology is the scientific study of birds (field of study : subject). Seismology is the study of earthquakes ✓ (Greek seismos = shaking).
seasons and seeds are sound traps ('se-'). oceans → oceanography.

q: Select the pair that best expresses a relationship similar to that expressed in the pair Pen : Write.
solution:
Bridge: a pen is used to write (tool : its function). A knife is used to cut ✓.
Book : Library = item : place where kept. Hammer : Carpenter = tool : user. Ink : Pen = material : the tool that holds it.

q: Select the pair that best expresses a relationship similar to that expressed in the pair Carpenter : Saw.
solution:
Bridge: a carpenter uses a saw (worker : tool), in that order. A surgeon uses a scalpel ✓.
Brush : Painter and Plough : Farmer have the right relation in the reverse order (tool : worker). Doctor : Hospital = worker : workplace.
Trap: direction matters — A : B must match C : D in the same order.

q:
Select the word that completes the analogy:
Generosity : Philanthropist :: Agility : __________
solution:
Bridge: generosity is the defining quality of a philanthropist (quality : person known for it). agility (ability to move quickly and easily) is the defining quality of an acrobat ✓.
A judge is known for impartiality, a banker for financial skill, a poet for imagination — not agility.

q:
Select the word that completes the analogy:
Fever : Infection :: Smoke : __________
solution:
Bridge: fever is a sign that indicates an infection (symptom/effect : the cause it points to). Smoke is a sign that indicates fire ✓.
pollution is caused by smoke — the direction is reversed (smoke → pollution, but fever ← infection). chimney is where smoke leaves a building. fog merely looks like smoke.
Trap: the cause–effect direction must match.

q:
Select the word that completes the analogy:
Ascend : Descend :: Augment : __________
solution:
Bridge: ascend (go up) is the opposite of descend (go down). augment = make greater; its opposite is diminish = make smaller ✓.
increase is a synonym of augment. argue is a sound trap ('aug/arg'). assemble is unrelated.

q:
Select the word that completes the analogy:
Dislike : Abhor :: Like : __________
solution:
Bridge: abhor is the extreme degree of dislike (mild : intense form of the same feeling). The extreme degree of like is adore ✓.
prefer and accept are mild — not the intense form. detest is the intense form of dislike, i.e. it belongs to the first pair's scale.

q:
Select the word that completes the analogy:
Negligence : Accident :: Practice : __________
solution:
Bridge: negligence leads to an accident (cause : result). practice leads to proficiency (skill) ✓.
rehearsal is a kind of practice — a synonym, not a result. practitioner is the person who practises. routine is a regular procedure, not an outcome of practice.

q:
Select the word that completes the analogy:
Umbrella : Rain :: Sunscreen : __________
solution:
Bridge: an umbrella protects against rain (protective item : what it guards against). Sunscreen protects against ultraviolet rays ✓.
skin is what sunscreen protects — that would match 'Umbrella : Person', a different relation. beach is a place of use. lotion is what sunscreen is (its form).
Trap: 'thing protected' vs 'thing protected against'.

q:
Select the word that completes the analogy:
Mumble : Speak :: Scrawl : __________
solution:
Bridge: to mumble is to speak indistinctly (a careless, unclear way of doing the action). To scrawl is to write in a hurried, careless way ✓.
draw: a scrawl is untidy writing, not a manner of drawing. read and erase are different actions.
Bridge sentence: 'to A is to B unclearly'.

q: Select the pair that best expresses a relationship similar to that expressed in the pair Jockey : Horse.
solution:
Bridge: a jockey rides and controls a horse (operator : what he steers). A pilot flies and controls an aircraft ✓.
Passenger : Train: a passenger rides but does not control — the key part of the relation is missing. Mechanic : Engine: repairs, does not operate. Hangar : Aeroplane: shelter : thing sheltered.
Trap: 'rides on' alone is too weak a bridge — make it specific.

q:
Select the word that completes the analogy:
Atlas : Maps :: Anthology : __________
solution:
Bridge: an atlas is a collection of maps (collection : items collected). An anthology is a collection of poems (or other pieces of writing) ✓.
poet, editor and publisher are people who write, compile or publish — not the items collected.

q:
Select the word that completes the analogy:
Archipelago : Islands :: Constellation : __________
solution:
Bridge: an archipelago is a group of islands (group : members). A constellation is a group of stars forming a recognised pattern ✓.
planets are not the members of constellations (they wander across them). sky is where constellations are seen; telescope is an instrument.

q: Select the pair that best expresses a relationship similar to that expressed in the pair Drought : Famine.
solution:
Bridge: a drought causes famine (cause : effect, in that order). Deforestation causes soil erosion ✓.
Famine : Drought = the same words in reverse (effect : cause). Rain : Cloud = effect : source, also reversed. Hunger : Food = need : the thing that satisfies it.
Trap: reversed order and 'same words, different relation'.

q: If '→' denotes increasing order of intensity, then the meaning of the words [drizzle → rain → downpour] is analogous to [breeze → __________ → hurricane]. Which one of the given options is appropriate to fill the blank?
solution:
First chain: rainfall growing heavier. Second chain: wind growing stronger, with the blank between a breeze (gentle wind) and a hurricane (violent storm).
gale = a very strong wind ✓.
zephyr = a soft, gentle breeze — weaker than a breeze, so it cannot sit between breeze and hurricane. lull = a temporary calm (absence of wind). mist is not wind at all.
Trap: the blank must be on the same scale and between its neighbours.

q: If '→' denotes increasing order of intensity, then the meaning of the words [pleased → delighted → ecstatic] is analogous to [displeased → __________ → furious]. Which one of the given options is appropriate to fill the blank?
solution:
First chain: happiness increasing. Second: displeasure increasing, with the blank between displeased (mildly unhappy with something) and furious (extremely angry).
angry ✓.
content (satisfied) and serene (calm) are on the opposite side of the scale. wistful = vaguely longing or sad — a different emotion.

q: If '→' denotes increasing order of intensity, then the meaning of the words [nibble → eat → devour] is analogous to [sip → __________ → guzzle]. Which one of the given options is appropriate to fill the blank?
solution:
First chain: eating, from tiny bites to eating greedily. Second: drinking, from a sip (a small mouthful) to guzzle (drink greedily in large amounts). The neutral middle word is drink ✓, just as 'eat' is in the first chain.
gnaw = bite persistently — an eating word. taste is not a degree of drinking. spill is unrelated to consuming.

q: If '→' denotes increasing order of intensity, then the meaning of the words [chilly → cold → frigid] is analogous to [warm → __________ → sweltering]. Which one of the given options is appropriate to fill the blank?
solution:
First chain: increasing coldness. Second: increasing heat from warm to sweltering (uncomfortably hot). The middle step is hot ✓.
tepid = only slightly warm — weaker than warm, so it cannot follow it. cool belongs to the cold side. humid describes moisture, not degree of heat.

q: If '→' denotes increasing order of intensity, then the meaning of the words [chuckle → laugh → guffaw] is analogous to [smile → __________ → beam]. Which one of the given options is appropriate to fill the blank?
solution:
First chain: laughter growing louder (chuckle = quiet laugh, guffaw = loud, hearty laugh). Second: a happy facial expression growing broader, from smile to beam (a very wide, radiant smile). In between is grin = a broad smile ✓.
frown and pout express displeasure. sneer = a contemptuous smile — a different emotion, not a stronger degree of happiness.

q: If '→' denotes increasing order of intensity, then the meaning of the words [annoy → anger → enrage] is analogous to [please → __________ → enrapture]. Which one of the given options is appropriate to fill the blank?
solution:
First chain: causing increasing degrees of anger. Second: causing increasing degrees of pleasure, up to enrapture (fill with intense delight). The middle step is delight = please greatly ✓.
appease = pacify by giving in to demands — it calms someone, but it is not a stronger form of pleasing. irritate belongs to the first chain's scale. bore is the opposite direction.
Trap: 'appease' looks like 'please' but works on a different scale (anger reduced, not joy increased).

q: If '→' denotes increasing order of intensity, then the meaning of the words [tiff → quarrel → feud] is analogous to [ripple → __________ → tsunami]. Which one of the given options is appropriate to fill the blank?
solution:
First chain: conflict growing in seriousness (a tiff is a petty quarrel, a feud a prolonged bitter one). Second: a disturbance on water growing in size, from a small ripple to a giant tsunami. The middle step is wave ✓.
tide = the regular rise and fall of the sea — not a size of wave. current = a flow of water in one direction. splash is a brief scattering of liquid, not a wave form.

q: If '→' denotes increasing order of intensity, then the meaning of the words [trickle → stream → torrent] is analogous to [glimmer → __________ → blaze]. Which one of the given options is appropriate to fill the blank?
solution:
First chain: flow of water increasing. Second: light increasing, from a glimmer (faint, wavering light) to a blaze (very bright flame or light). The middle step is glow = a steady, moderate light ✓.
shade and dusk are reductions of light, not degrees of it. smoke goes with fire but is not light.

q: If '→' denotes increasing order of intensity, then the meaning of the words [decline → slump → crash] is analogous to [rise → __________ → skyrocket]. Which one of the given options is appropriate to fill the blank?
solution:
First chain: falling, increasingly sharply (e.g. prices). Second: rising, increasingly sharply, up to skyrocket (rise very steeply and fast). The middle step is surge = a sudden powerful rise ✓.
dip = a small fall — opposite direction. plateau and stagnate = stop changing — no rise at all.

q: If '→' denotes increasing order of closeness in a relationship, which one of the following chains is correct?
solution:
acquaintance = a person one knows slightly; friend = a person one knows well and likes; confidant = a close, trusted friend with whom one shares secrets.
Increasing closeness: acquaintance → friend → confidant ✓.
The second option is the same chain reversed (decreasing). The others misplace 'acquaintance' or 'confidant'.

q: If '→' denotes increasing order of intensity, which one of the following chains is NOT correctly ordered?
solution:
Check each chain:
content (satisfied) → happy → elated (very happy, exhilarated): increasing ✓.
spark → flame → blaze (a large, fierce fire): increasing ✓.
unease (slight anxiety) → fear → terror (extreme fear): increasing ✓.
furious → angry → annoyed runs from strongest to weakest — it is decreasing, so it is the one not correctly ordered ✓.
Trap: reading 'NOT' and still picking a correct chain.

q: If '→' denotes increasing order of intensity, then the meaning of the words [interest → enthusiasm → obsession] is analogous to [concern → __________ → panic]. Which one of the given options is appropriate to fill the blank?
solution:
First chain: involvement growing until it is excessive (obsession). Second: worry growing from mild concern to panic (sudden uncontrollable fear). The middle step is anxiety = intense worry ✓.
apathy (lack of interest) and relief (removal of worry) are on the other side. curiosity belongs to the interest scale, not the worry scale.

q:
__________ is to architect as recipe is to __________
Which one of the following options maintains a similar logical relation in the above sentence?
solution:
Fill from the known half: a recipe is the written plan that a chef works from. The first blank must be the written plan of an architect — a blueprint ✓.
Building, kitchen: an architect designs a building, but a recipe is not 'to a kitchen' in that way (a kitchen is a place). Pencil, food: tool and product, mixed. Client, waiter: people, not plans.
Shortcut: test both blanks in one bridge sentence — 'A ___ is the plan an architect works from; a recipe is the plan a ___ works from'.

q:
Bird : P :: Fish : Q
Which one of the following P and Q combinations forms a meaningful analogy?
solution:
Bridge: feathers cover a bird's body; scales cover a fish's body (animal : body covering) ✓.
Wings / Swim: a body part paired with an action. Fly / Gills: an action paired with a body part. Nest / Fins: a home paired with a body part. Each mixes two different relations, so the halves do not match.
Rule: P and Q must stand in the same relation and be the same kind of word.

q:
Sculptor : P :: Poet : Q
Which one of the following P and Q combinations forms a meaningful analogy?
solution:
Bridge: a sculptor creates a statue; a poet creates a poem (artist : work created) ✓.
Chisel / Verse: a chisel is the sculptor's tool, but verse is the poet's product — tool on one side, product on the other. Museum / Rhyme: a place paired with a feature of poems. Stone / Library: material paired with a place.
Trap: an option that looks right in one half only.

q:
Pen : Writer :: __________ : __________
Select the pair that completes the analogy.
solution:
Bridge: a pen is the tool used by a writer (tool : user, in that order). A brush is the tool used by a painter ✓.
Painter : Brush = correct words in reverse order (user : tool). Canvas : Paint = surface : material. Paint : Wall = material : surface.
Trap: order reversal.

q:
__________ is to illness as education is to __________
Which one of the following options maintains a similar logical relation in the above sentence?
solution:
Bridge: medicine removes illness; education removes ignorance (remedy : what it removes) ✓.
Doctor, school: a doctor treats illness, but education does not 'treat' a school. Cure, knowledge: 'cure is to illness' is plausible, but 'education is to knowledge' is remedy : result, not remedy : problem — the two halves differ. Hospital, teacher: place and person, mismatched.
Trap: an option whose first half fits but whose second half switches the relation.

q:
Library : P :: Museum : Q
Which one of the following P and Q combinations forms a meaningful analogy?
solution:
Bridge: a library houses a collection of books; a museum houses a collection of artefacts (institution : what it keeps) ✓.
Librarian / Exhibits: a person on one side, objects on the other. Reading / Curator: an activity paired with a person. Silence / Tickets: unrelated features.

q: Select all pairs that have the same relationship as Herbivore : Plants.
solution:
Bridge: a herbivore is an animal that feeds on plants.
Carnivore feeds on flesh ✓. Insectivore feeds on insects ✓.
Scavenger : Hunter — a scavenger feeds on dead animals; it does not feed on hunters ✗. Teetotaller : Alcohol — a teetotaller abstains from alcohol, the opposite relation ✗.

q: Select all pairs that have the same relationship as Ornithologist : Birds.
solution:
Bridge: an ornithologist is a person who studies birds (specialist : subject of study).
Entomologist studies insects ✓. Numismatist studies (and collects) coins ✓.
Cartographer : Maps — a cartographer makes maps (worker : product) ✗. Astronomer : Telescope — worker : tool; an astronomer studies celestial objects, using a telescope ✗.

q: Select all pairs that have the same relationship as Obstinate : Stubborn.
solution:
Obstinate and stubborn are synonyms.
Lucid = clear ✓ (synonyms). Lethargic = sluggish, lacking energy ✓ (synonyms).
Prudent (careful, sensible) vs rash (acting without thought) — antonyms ✗. Ample (more than enough) vs scarce — antonyms ✗.

q: Select all pairs that have the same relationship as Verbose : Concise.
solution:
Verbose (using more words than needed) and concise (brief and clear) are antonyms.
Opulent (rich, luxurious) vs impoverished (very poor) — antonyms ✓. Benevolent (well-meaning, kind) vs malevolent (wishing harm) — antonyms ✓.
Arid and parched (both = very dry) — synonyms ✗. Tranquil and serene (both = calm) — synonyms ✗.

q: Select all pairs that have the same relationship as Illegible : Read.
solution:
Bridge: something illegible cannot be read (adjective : the action that cannot be done to it).
Inaudible = cannot be heard ✓. Invisible = cannot be seen ✓.
Inedible = cannot be eaten, not 'cannot be cooked' ✗. Indelible = cannot be erased; indelible ink can certainly be written with ✗.
Trap: the in-/il- prefix fits all four; the verb must be exactly the action that is impossible.
